title: Pendulum

slow_motion.evidence: no captions, narration or visual cues indicate slow motion

subjects.description: small red spherical bob hanging from a thin black string

observation.what_happens: A red ball on a thin string swings back and forth under a horizontal support beside a striped vertical scale. It begins displaced to the right, swings left through bottom-dead-center and continues oscillating for the whole clip.

calibration.note: no ruler needed: the swing is measured as an angle

given: g = 9.807 m/s² (Earth): hold g fixed and measure the pendulum's length L in metres from its swing
reasoning: Theta is a ~0.14 rad sine with ~1.55 s period and slight amplitude decay, and the path is a clean circle, so it is a pendulum of L ~0.6 m. Candidates go from ideal small-angle to linear viscous damping to full sine plus quadratic air drag to test what causes the decay.

law.summary: A tiny-angle swing that slowly dies out because air drag is proportional to speed.

caveats: Length in metres rests on holding Earth gravity fixed; video alone gives shape only.
Small-angle form assumes modest swings and ignores sine correction.
String and support are taken as ideal with no stretch or wobble.
critique.finding: The ball swings on a string of length {L}. Light viscous drag {b} slowly steals its swing.
critique.headline: The ball swings steadily while air gently slows it.
critique.why_it_won: It keeps the swing size fading evenly, while quadratic drag would fade big swings too fast and small swings too slowly.

headline: The ball swings steadily while air gently slows it.
finding: The ball swings on a string of length 0.601 ± 7.75e-5 m. Light viscous drag 0.0491 ± 5.54e-4 1/s slowly steals its swing.

eyeball.confidence: low - length from apparent meter-stick stripes and ~1.5 s period, damping from barely perceptible amplitude loss over ~6 s; highly uncertain without calibrated scale and longer timing
eyeball.law_in_words: Small-angle pendulum T = 2*pi*sqrt(L/g) gives L from oscillation period, and for x'' + b*x' + (g/L)*x = 0 the amplitude envelope decays as exp(-b*t/2), so b is inferred from fractional amplitude decay over observed time.
